Recovering analytic data from harmonic fields

Original exposition and proofs: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. CC0.

An analytic functional on a real compact set can be observed from outside that set through a harmonic field in one extra dimension. The field changes sign on reflection across the original space. Its normal jump has the correct normalization for distributions, and a cutoff integral recovers every analytic test pairing. Conversely, every such odd harmonic field determines an analytic functional; the only ambiguity is an everywhere harmonic field. Requiring decay at infinity removes that ambiguity.

We write , , and use , bilinear pairings and ordinary derivatives. An analytic functional carried by a real compact has, for every complex neighborhood of , a bound . Analytic tests and real carriers, Theorems 1–6, proves polynomial determination, extension to holomorphic germs, parameter differentiation and the faithful inclusion of compact distributions. Those results are used below with their full neighborhood quantifiers.

The normalized Laplace fundamental solution and its first derivatives come from Point sources and complex Gaussian kernels, Theorem 1.1. Tensor products and parameter-dependent distributions and Convolution as addition of supports supply differentiation of compact pairings and convolution with one compact smooth factor. The angular reading, A4–A5, proves polar integration and sphere area; the Fourier reading, F3, proves the Gaussian integral. Gamma integrals and recurrence are in the gamma reading, G0–G2. The Cauchy reading, CMI6–CMI8, supplies the complex estimates and series used here. Cutoffs, calculus, dominated integration and Fubini are supplied by the metric and integration readings.

We also use an already proved regularity consequence. A harmonic distribution is real analytic: apply analytic differential regularity, Theorem 3, to the elliptic operator , then wavefront projection, Theorem 5, and the analytic derivative criterion, Proposition 3. Its convergent real Taylor series gives a local holomorphic extension satisfying the same equation. A harmonic function that is zero on an open part of a connected domain is therefore zero throughout: the set of points where all derivatives vanish is closed, is open by its Taylor series, and contains the initial open set. This argument applies to complex-valued functions as well.

The smallest real carrier

Theorem 6 (support detected by harmonic continuation). Every analytic functional with some real compact carrier has a unique smallest real compact carrier, denoted . A real compact set is a carrier exactly when the canonical field extends to a harmonic function on .

Proof. If is a carrier, Theorem 4 constructs the extension. Canonical fields computed from two carriers agree off the plane. To justify this without assuming uniqueness of a germ extension on unrelated sets, use their compact union: the kernel at is holomorphic near that union, and entire approximation there makes its pairing through either carrier the same limit. Unique continuation gives agreement wherever both fields are defined.

Conversely, suppose the canonical field extends across all points outside . The extension remains odd, since its reflection agrees off the plane. It tends to zero at infinity. Theorem 5 gives whose canonical field is exactly this extension, with no entire harmonic term. Regard as carried by the union of an original carrier and . Its canonical field is zero outside that union, so injectivity in Theorem 4 gives . Thus is a carrier.

Now let be the intersection of all real compact carriers of . It is a compact subset of any one of them. The compatible fields for these carriers glue on the union of their domains, which is exactly the complement of . Harmonicity is local, so the glued field is harmonic there and still tends to zero at infinity. The criterion just proved gives . This also covers the empty intersection: the glued field is globally harmonic and tends to zero, hence is zero, and injectivity gives . Minimality and uniqueness follow from the definition of the intersection.

This is a statement about real carriers. The disjoint complex-carrier example in the preceding lesson remains valid.

Exercise 8 — why the oddness assumption matters. Take the even field in (P1), harmonic off the origin. Show that the recovery expression using odd lifts and an even cutoff gives zero, although cannot extend harmonically through the origin.

Solution. The lift is odd, so is odd when is even. Multiplication by the even gives an odd compact integrand supported away from zero, whose integral is zero. Thus these normal-data tests detect nothing. Nevertheless the locally integrable satisfies . If it agreed off zero with a smooth harmonic extension, the two locally integrable functions would agree almost everywhere, hence define the same distribution, contradicting this point source. Even singular fields therefore cannot be included in Theorem 5 with the same normal-data construction.

Mathematical source

Lars Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I, second edition, 2003 reprint, Section 9.1, Propositions 9.1.3 and 9.1.5, Lemma 9.1.4 and Theorem 9.1.6. The harmonic lift uses spherical directional estimates; its converse uses a compact smooth source and harmonic Taylor polynomials.
